title: 2 Chronicles 35:1–19
context: In the eighteenth year of his reign Josiah keeps the Passover in Jerusalem on the fourteenth day of the first month, setting the priests in their offices and directing the Levites to serve according to the writing of David and Solomon and the LORD’s word by Moses. The king and his officials provide thousands of animals for the people, the priests and Levites carry out the service in order, and the singers and gatekeepers remain at their posts. Both traditions read this as shared ground on worship renewed by the word; 2 Kings 23:21–23 gives a shorter account of the same Passover.

verses.text: Josiah kept a Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem. They killed the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Josiah kept a Passover to the LORD in Jerusalem. They killed the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month.” Arminian readers note that the date follows the law’s appointed time (Exod 12:6; Lev 23:5).

Hezekiah’s Passover had been kept in the second month (2 Chr 30:2).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see worship ordered by God’s word rather than by convenience.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the Passover remembers the LORD’s redemption from Egypt, and Josiah’s reform is completed by joyful worship, not only by removing idols.

verses.text: He set the priests in their offices and encouraged them in the service of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He set the priests in their offices and encouraged them in the service of the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers note that Josiah both organizes and encourages those who serve.

Reform involves people as well as structures.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the king supporting the priesthood God had appointed.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: faithful leaders strengthen those who serve in worship, rather than only giving orders.

verses.text: He said to the Levites who taught all Israel, who were holy to the LORD, “Put the holy ark in the house which Solomon the son of David king of Israel built. It will no longer be a burden on your shoulders. Now serve the LORD your God and his people Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Josiah tells the Levites, “Put the holy ark in the house which Solomon the son of David king of Israel built. It will no longer be a burden on your shoulders.” Arminian readers note the shift in the Levites’ role now that the ark rests in the temple (cf. 1 Chr 23:26).

Why the ark needed to be put back is not explained.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the Levites redirected to “serve the LORD your God and his people Israel.”

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: service to God and service to his people belong together, and the text does not say where the ark had been.

verses.text: Prepare yourselves after your fathers’ houses by your divisions, according to the writing of David king of Israel, and according to the writing of Solomon his son.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Prepare yourselves after your fathers” houses by your divisions, according to the writing of David king of Israel, and according to the writing of Solomon his son.’ Arminian readers note that the reform follows the order established earlier (1 Chr 23–26; 2 Chr 8:14).

Continuity with the past guides renewal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see worship arranged according to God-given patterns handed down through David and Solomon.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the Chronicler presents the temple service as rooted in an inherited, ordered tradition.

verses.text: Stand in the holy place according to the divisions of the fathers’ houses of your brothers the children of the people, and let there be for each a portion of a fathers’ house of the Levites.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Stand in the holy place according to the divisions of the fathers” houses of your brothers the children of the people.’ Arminian readers note that each family group is served by Levites.

The arrangement ensures that all the people are cared for.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the care taken that the whole people share in the Passover.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: order in worship serves the participation of everyone, not the privilege of a few.

verses.text: Kill the Passover lamb, sanctify yourselves, and prepare for your brothers, to do according to the LORD’s word by Moses.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Kill the Passover lamb, sanctify yourselves, and prepare for your brothers, to do according to the LORD’s word by Moses.” Arminian readers note the call to personal holiness alongside the ritual.

The Levites serve on behalf of their brothers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the Passover kept according to the word given through Moses.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: worship is shaped by God’s word, and those who lead it must first sanctify themselves.

verses.text: Josiah gave to the children of the people, of the flock, lambs and young goats, all of them for the Passover offerings, to all who were present, to the number of thirty thousand, and three thousand bulls. These were of the king’s substance.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Josiah gave to the children of the people, of the flock, lambs and young goats... to the number of thirty thousand, and three thousand bulls. These were of the king’s substance.” Arminian readers note the king’s generosity from his own possessions.

The king gives so that the people can take part.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see generous provision for the people’s worship, much as David gave from his own treasure (1 Chr 29:3).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: leaders who give freely make worship possible for others.

verses.text: His princes gave a free will offering to the people, to the priests, and to the Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the rulers of God’s house, gave to the priests for the Passover offerings two thousand six hundred small livestock, and three hundred head of cattle.
verses.arminianNotes:
“His princes gave a free will offering to the people, to the priests, and to the Levites.” Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel also give to the priests. Arminian readers note that the king’s example is followed by others.

Hilkiah is the priest who found the book of the law (34:14).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see willing generosity spreading through the leadership.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: freewill offerings express joy in God’s renewed covenant.

verses.text: Conaniah also, and Shemaiah and Nethanel, his brothers, and Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, the chiefs of the Levites, gave to the Levites for the Passover offerings five thousand small livestock and five hundred head of cattle.
verses.arminianNotes:
The chiefs of the Levites “gave to the Levites for the Passover offerings five thousand small livestock and five hundred head of cattle.” Arminian readers note that the Levite leaders provide for their own.

Each group of leaders contributes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the same willing spirit among the Levites.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the list of names honors those who gave, and the Passover is supplied by many hands.

verses.text: So the service was prepared, and the priests stood in their place, and the Levites by their divisions, according to the king’s commandment.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the service was prepared, and the priests stood in their place, and the Levites by their divisions, according to the king’s commandment.” Arminian readers note the readiness of all who served.

Preparation precedes worship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see order in the service of God’s house.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: careful preparation is a form of reverence, and each person has a place.

verses.text: They killed the Passover lambs, and the priests sprinkled the blood which they received from their hands, and the Levites skinned them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They killed the Passover lambs, and the priests sprinkled the blood which they received from their hands, and the Levites skinned them.” Arminian readers note the cooperation between priests and Levites (cf. 2 Chr 30:16).

Each group does its part.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the blood of the Passover at the center of the rite, recalling the LORD’s redemption (Exod 12:13).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, and both see the Passover fulfilled in Christ, “our Passover” (1 Cor 5:7), as a reading the New Testament supplies.

verses.text: They removed the burnt offerings, that they might give them according to the divisions of the fathers’ houses of the children of the people, to offer to the LORD, as it is written in the book of Moses. They did the same with the cattle.
verses.arminianNotes:
They distribute the burnt offerings by family groups “to offer to the LORD, as it is written in the book of Moses.” Arminian readers note that the people themselves take part in offering.

The service follows the written law.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the repeated appeal to what is written.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the Chronicler presents faithful worship as obedience to Scripture.

verses.text: They roasted the Passover with fire according to the ordinance. They boiled the holy offerings in pots, in cauldrons, and in pans, and carried them quickly to all the children of the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They roasted the Passover with fire according to the ordinance.” The holy offerings are boiled and carried quickly to the people. Arminian readers note care for both the law (Exod 12:8–9) and the people’s needs.

The service is efficient and generous.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see attention to the ordinance in every detail.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: worship is both obedient and hospitable, as food is brought quickly to all the people.

verses.text: Afterward they prepared for themselves and for the priests, because the priests the sons of Aaron were busy with offering the burnt offerings and the fat until night. Therefore the Levites prepared for themselves and for the priests the sons of Aaron.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Afterward they prepared for themselves and for the priests,” because the priests were busy with the offerings until night. Arminian readers note the Levites’ willingness to serve others first.

They provide for the priests who could not leave their work.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see mutual care among those who serve.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: service in God’s house includes looking after fellow workers.

verses.text: The singers, the sons of Asaph, were in their place, according to the commandment of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun the king’s seer; and the gatekeepers were at every gate. They didn’t need to depart from their service, because their brothers the Levites prepared for them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The singers, the sons of Asaph, were in their place “according to the commandment of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun the king’s seer” (cf. 1 Chr 25:1). Arminian readers note that music has its place in worship.

The Levites prepare for the singers and gatekeepers so they need not leave their posts.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the singers and gatekeepers serving in the order David established.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: different gifts serve together, and each can remain faithful at its post because others support it.

verses.text: So all the service of the LORD was prepared the same day, to keep the Passover, and to offer burnt offerings on the LORD’s altar, according to the commandment of King Josiah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So all the service of the LORD was prepared the same day, to keep the Passover, and to offer burnt offerings on the LORD’s altar.” Arminian readers note the completeness of the preparation.

The king’s command is carried out fully.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the day’s worship completed as directed.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the Chronicler highlights a unified and complete act of worship.

verses.text: The children of Israel who were present kept the Passover at that time, and the feast of unleavened bread seven days.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The children of Israel who were present kept the Passover at that time, and the feast of unleavened bread seven days.” Arminian readers note the people’s participation in the full festival (Exod 12:15).

The celebration lasts a week.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the whole festival kept as God appointed.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the people join in remembering the LORD’s deliverance.

verses.text: There was no Passover like that kept in Israel from the days of Samuel the prophet, nor did any of the kings of Israel keep such a Passover as Josiah kept—with the priests, the Levites, and all Judah and Israel who were present, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“There was no Passover like that kept in Israel from the days of Samuel the prophet.” Arminian readers note the significance of the celebration.

2 Kings 23:22 says “from the days of the judges”; the two books use different reference points.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the Passover as a high point of Josiah’s reform, involving “all Judah and Israel who were present.”

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and read the two accounts side by side, consistent with the notes on 2 Kings 23:22.

verses.text: This Passover was kept in the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah.
verses.arminianNotes:
“This Passover was kept in the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah.” Arminian readers note that the date matches 2 Kings 23:23 and the year the book of the law was found (34:8).

Renewal follows quickly on the discovery of the word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the same year marking both discovery and celebration.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God’s word, once recovered, leads to renewed worship.
